# Submission to the Senate Community Affairs Legislation Committee

## National Disability Insurance Scheme Amendment (Securing the NDIS for Future Generations) Bill 2026

Submitted by: Jarrod Hamilton Role: Self-managed NDIS participant, independent researcher Date: May 2026 Position on the Bill: Serious concerns

This submission is made at a critical juncture. The Bill before the committee presents as a sustainability and integrity measure. What it actually is is a cost-containment exercise conducted on a scheme whose structural problems have never been correctly named, let alone fixed. The difference matters enormously, because cost-containment applied to a structurally broken system does not fix the structure. It concentrates the damage on the people least able to absorb it.

The stakes are not abstract. For participants like me, they are immediate, material, and compounding. This submission names the structural problems, proposes a specific mechanism to address the pricing architecture failure at the scheme's core, and asks the committee to hold both dimensions clearly: the scheme must be sustainable, and it must actually work for the people it exists to serve. Those are not competing objectives unless the governance architecture is broken. This submission argues it is, and explains why.

-----

## 1\. Introduction

I have thousands of dollars in NDIS funding I am structurally unable to spend. Not because my needs are not real. Because the system has no mechanism to tell me what I am allowed to buy, at what price, from whom, or why. That is not a participant failing to navigate the scheme. That is the scheme failing to be navigable.

I am a self-managed participant living with Multiple Sclerosis, with foot drop, heat-induced muscle spasms, chronic fatigue, brain fog, and short-term memory impairment. The last of those makes navigating a system that is deliberately complex not a bureaucratic inconvenience but a clinical barrier. I barely use my plan's funding. Not from lack of need. From fear of getting a call up and having to pay something back.

The NDIS was designed as insurance for two things simultaneously: having a disability, and supporting the workforce that serves those who do. Both purposes were legitimate. Both remain legitimate. What the scheme became in practice is something the name never captured and the governance architecture was never built to handle: a national disability support infrastructure, underwriting not just individual participants but an entire care economy, on the pricing assumptions of a tightly bounded insurance product. The name never updated. The governance never updated. The cost trajectory was the predictable result.

The Bill before this committee is the latest attempt to address that trajectory. It does so by tightening compliance, restricting eligibility pathways, and adding administrative requirements to participant interactions with the scheme. Some of those measures are necessary. None of them address the fundamental pricing architecture failure that makes the scheme simultaneously expensive and unusable for a significant proportion of its participants.

This submission is that experience made structural, and a proposal for the specific mechanism the Bill requires but does not include.

What I find genuinely staggering is that a system incapable of funding a tennis court hire, only the support worker to watch me watch other people play, has simultaneously managed to become one of the most fraud-ridden public programs in Australian history. That contradiction is not an accident. It is the direct result of a pricing architecture with no floor on what can be extracted and no ceiling on what can be obscured. The structural problems elaborated in this submission are the product of an investigation I would never have undertaken had the government not proposed these changes. So I suppose I should say thank you. What I found was a neglected and fully outsourced workforce worse than Uber Eats.

Now do try to keep up.

# Strategic Analysis: Socioeconomic Sieges and the "Fight or Die" Threshold in Liquid Fuel Starvation

## 1\. Introduction: The Mechanics of the Socioeconomic Siege

The traditional concept of military siege warfare involves surrounding a physical location to prevent the ingress of supplies, slowly starving the inhabitants into submission. In the highly interconnected, hyper-globalized framework of the 21st century, this physical encirclement is no longer required. A state can be besieged remotely. The weaponization of maritime chokepoints, such as the Strait of Hormuz in 2026, constitutes a modern "socioeconomic siege."

By severing the arteries of global liquid fuel, an aggressor does not need to fire a single shot at the target nation's mainland. Instead, they weaponize the target nation's own thermodynamic dependencies against it. Modern industrial society is not merely reliant on oil; it is entirely constructed from it. When the inflow of diesel and petrol ceases, the internal mechanisms of the state, agricultural production, logistics, and eventually social cohesion, begin to cannibalize themselves. This document analyzes the mathematical inevitability of the "fight or die" threshold, detailing how quickly a nation transitions from civilian panic to kinetic military desperation when subjected to energy starvation.

## 2\. The Illusion of Reserves and the Mathematics of Panic

The fundamental vulnerability of a nation like Australia under a socioeconomic siege is the illusion of its strategic reserves. Official government statistics frequently cite roughly 30 to 35 days of liquid fuel consumption cover. This metric represents a catastrophic misunderstanding of logistics. It treats fuel "on the water" (in transit across the ocean) and fuel heavily centralized in coastal import terminals as if it were readily available at the local retail node.

When a geopolitical shock occurs, the psychological reaction of the civilian population compresses the timeline of failure. The behavioral thermodynamics of panic buying dictate that the population shifts from "just-in-time" purchasing to "just-in-case" hoarding.

### The Cascading Failure Matrix:

  - The Retail Wipeout: The average civilian vehicle holds between 50 and 80 litres. If the public decides to keep their tanks full rather than waiting until they are nearly empty, the localized demand spikes by a factor of three to five. The underground tanks at local service stations, which are designed to hold only 48 to 72 hours of baseline supply, are drained in less than two days.
  - The Logistics Fracture: The physical chokepoint is not the amount of fuel in the country, but the number of tanker trucks available to move it. There are finite heavy vehicles and licensed drivers available to distribute fuel from the coastal terminals to the 8,000 retail stations nationwide. When every station runs dry simultaneously, the distribution grid is hopelessly backlogged.
  - The Regional Triage: As the logistics network fractures, centralized distributors enact brutal triage protocols. Priority is given to major urban centers to prevent immediate political collapse, leaving regional arteries critically starved. For critical freight routes like the Newell Highway running through Coonabarabran, the absence of diesel paralyzes the movement of food, pharmaceuticals, and agricultural machinery.

By front-loading demand, the civilian population effectively traps millions of litres of fuel inside private vehicles, rendering it useless to the broader economic grid. The 35-day national reserve is a statistical phantom; systemic retail failure occurs within 14 to 20 days.

## 3\. Historical Isomorphisms: The Speed to Retaliation (The "Fight" Aspect)

The thermodynamic reality of state survival dictates that a government cannot allow its agricultural and logistics grids to fail completely. When the mathematical certainty of starvation becomes undeniable, the state is forced into the "fight or die" paradigm. Historical isomorphisms demonstrate that the timeline between the initiation of a severe energy embargo and the deployment of kinetic military force is brutally consistent, typically falling within a 90 to 120 day window. # Epistemic Approximation: A Formal Analysis of Belief, Language, and Ground Truth

## 1\. The Ontological Metric: Reality as a Complete State

To formulate a quantitative ontology of knowledge, fundamental reality regarding any phenomenon can be defined as an exhaustive, invariant state of unity, represented by $T = 1.0$ (or $100%$ ). Under this definition, absolute truth is not an ethereal concept or a subjective evaluation; it is the total, uncompressed sum of all actual properties, constituent particles, energetic relationships, and causal dynamics governing a system across time. This ground truth exists completely independent of an observer's presence, cognitive capacity, or linguistic capability. It operates as the invariant boundary condition of the cosmos, self-sufficient and fully determined.

Human cognition, by contrast, cannot contain or instantiate the referent itself. A human mind observing an orbital trajectory or the combustion of fuel does not host the planetary mass or the exothermic reaction; it hosts only an informational proxy. Consequently, any cognitive representation or communicative articulation of that reality is necessarily an incomplete subset, designated here as a scalar magnitude $n$ , bounded by the closed interval:

$$ 0 \\le n \\le 1.0 $$

The central problem of epistemology lies in the structural mechanics that govern the generation, transmission, and recalibration of $n$ , and in the profound barrier that prevents an observer from directly reading its true value.

## 2\. The Informational Gradient: Internal Belief and External Articulation

The epistemic agent interacts with absolute ground truth through a sequence of cascading translations, each marked by information loss, compression, and systemic degradation. These transitions create two distinct ontological categories of information: internal belief and external statement.

Ground Truth (T = 1.0)

│

▼ \[Perceptual & Cognitive Compression\]

Internal Belief (n\_internal)

│

▼ \[Semiotic Encoding & Transmission Loss\]

External Statement (n\_external)

### The Architecture of Internal Information ( $n\_{\\text{internal}}$ )

Belief represents an internal informational state—a neurocomputational model, conceptual schema, or perceptual map generated within an observer's cognitive architecture. The mind cannot intake the infinite density of physical reality because biological sensory systems operate under strict bandwidth, latency, and resolution limits. Retinal cells capture only a narrow electromagnetic band; auditory systems register only a localized spectrum of pressure waves; cognitive processing capacity operates under sharp metabolic and architectural boundaries.

To make sense of sensory input, cognition must discard the overwhelming majority of raw data, relying on predictive heuristics, selective filtering, and conceptual categorization. The resulting mental model is an aggressively compressed projection of the external referent. When an individual holds a belief about an object or principle, this internal belief ( $n\_{\\text{internal}}$ ) inevitably excludes microscopic variables, causal nuances, and context-dependent anomalies. Because compression inherently involves variable omission, an internal belief is mathematically constrained such that:

$$ n\_{\\text{internal}} \< 1.0 $$

Even in the most rigorous human thinker, an internal belief can approximate aspects of reality with high fidelity, yet it remains structurally distinct from the reality it seeks to map.

### The Degradation of External Information ( $n\_{\\text{external}}$ )

When an agent attempts to transmit an internal belief to another mind or record it in an objective medium, a secondary translation occurs: the belief must be externalized into symbolic syntax, spoken acoustics, mathematical notation, or physical gesture. This is the domain of the statement ( $n\_{\\text{external}}$ ).

While internal beliefs suffer from perceptual and cognitive compression, external statements suffer from the constraints of semiotic encoding and transmission fidelity. Language is inherently contextual, discrete, and lossy. A word or formal symbol is a generalized token that attempts to capture a rich, multidimensional cognitive state. During this externalization, nuance is stripped away, syntax introduces ambiguities, and the subjective connotations embedded within the sender's neural landscape fail to cleanly imprint onto the symbolic output.

Furthermore, once projected into an external medium, the statement is subject to medium degradation and communicative friction, including reception bias and semantic drift...

# The Epistemic Allegory: An Information-Based Philosophy of Concept Generation

This document outlines an epistemological framework that reinterprets ancient historical, biological, and religious narratives as an intricate, functional language for information processing and idea generation. In this philosophy, the human being is conceptualized fundamentally as a vessel for information and belief. Consequently, physical entities, biological processes, and historical conflicts are viewed not merely as literal events, but as the primary analogical vocabulary available to ancient writers to communicate the rigorous management of internal knowledge. At the apex of this framework is the conception of the divine as an entity of pure information. Existing prior to physical reality and prior to the potential for a physical universe, this divine intellect operates outside the constraints of mortal observation. Because its native language is unadulterated data, the physical history of humanity functions as a translational layer—a concrete medium through which the mechanics of pure idea formation are communicated to physically grounded minds.

To understand why ancient narratives use physical actions to communicate abstract epistemological truths, one must grasp the ancient understanding of language itself. In modern Western epistemology, words are frequently treated as arbitrary, abstract signifiers that float above physical reality. In the ancient Semitic worldview, however, language is grounded strictly in observable action and effect. Words do not describe speculative abstractions; they describe tangible vectors of cause and consequence occurring within the physical theater.

This linguistic reality is crystallized in the foundational Hebrew noun dabar ( $\\text{דָּבָר}$ , Strong's H1697), which derives from the verbal root dabar ( $\\text{דָּבַר}$ , Strong's H1696), meaning "to speak, to arrange, to drive forward, or to lead." The language possesses no structural gap between an articulated concept and a concrete occurrence; a word is an initiated action, and an event is an articulated concept brought to effect. As linguistic philosopher Thorleif Boman demonstrated in his comparative studies of Hebrew and Greek thought, dynamic movement and energetic effect form the bedrock of ancient Near Eastern consciousness.

Because action and effect are the undeniable manifestations of reality that human perception can register, they constitute the only stable medium available to map internal, non-physical operations. When ancient authors set out to describe the invisible mechanics of the mind—such as hypothesis formation, bias reception, conceptual pruning, or cognitive corruption—they necessarily employed the dynamics of biological conception, bodily conflict, and manual cultivation. The physical event was not an arbitrary decoration; it was the direct kinetic embodiment of an information process.

Physical union is not a euphemism for knowledge; rather, cognitive apprehension is the primary operation, and physical union serves as its most visible earthly analogy.
